# ALS evidence packet — draft v1

This curated input is not a comprehensive review. Every method receives the same UTF-8 file. Summaries are original paraphrases. Bibliographic metadata and abstracts were checked through the public NCBI ID converter and PubMed EFetch on 2026-10-05. Selected studies predate 2025; this does not remove knowledge already in a model's training. Co-Scientist outputs are not included.

## Research question

Propose one specific, testable hypothesis connecting phosphorylation of a nuclear-pore-complex nucleoporin to ALS-related neuronal dysfunction. Explain the causal chain, distinguish an initiating mechanism from a downstream response, and propose an experimental strategy that discriminates the hypothesis from an alternative. Identify supported premises, speculative bridges, and a falsifying observation. This adapts Co-Scientist Supplementary Note 10; nucleoporin phosphorylation is not supplied as an established ALS cause.

## S1 — TDP-43 and nuclear-pore dysfunction

Chou et al. (2018), *TDP-43 pathology disrupts nuclear pore complexes and nucleocytoplasmic transport in ALS/FTD*. Nature Neuroscience. DOI: `10.1038/s41593-017-0047-3`; PMID: `29311743`; PMCID: `PMC5800968`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29311743/).

Nuclear-pore and transport components were associated with insoluble TDP-43 aggregates. Disease-linked TDP-43 disrupted nucleoporin localization and nuclear transport in experimental cell systems; relevant pore pathology was observed in ALS tissue. This supports examining the connection between TDP-43 pathology and transport disruption. It does not identify a nucleoporin phosphorylation event as the initiating cause or establish the same sequence in every ALS subtype.

## S2 — C9orf72-associated transport defects

Zhang et al. (2015), *The C9orf72 repeat expansion disrupts nucleocytoplasmic transport*. Nature. DOI: `10.1038/nature14973`; PMID: `26308891`; PMCID: `PMC4800742`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26308891/).

Expanded C9orf72 repeat RNA was linked to altered RanGAP localization and impaired nuclear import in models and patient-derived neurons. Manipulations of transport or repeat-RNA-associated mechanisms modified model phenotypes. This supplies a genetic-context-specific route to transport dysfunction. It does not show that sporadic ALS arises by the same route or directly establish a nucleoporin phosphorylation mechanism.

## S3 — A stress-granule-independent route

Gasset-Rosa et al. (2019), *Cytoplasmic TDP-43 De-mixing Independent of Stress Granules Drives Inhibition of Nuclear Import, Loss of Nuclear TDP-43, and Cell Death*. Neuron. DOI: `10.1016/j.neuron.2019.02.038`; PMID: `30853299`; PMCID: `PMC6548321`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30853299/).

Persistent cytoplasmic TDP-43 assemblies could form independently of conventional stress granules. They recruited or mislocalized transport-associated proteins and were associated with impaired transport, nuclear TDP-43 depletion, and cell death. Phosphorylated TDP-43 accumulated in these assemblies. That is not itself evidence of nucleoporin phosphorylation. The experimental perturbations do not establish that every physiological ALS trajectory begins in this way.

## S4 — A stress-granule-associated route

Zhang et al. (2018), *Stress Granule Assembly Disrupts Nucleocytoplasmic Transport*. Cell. DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2018.03.025`; PMID: `29628143`; PMCID: `PMC6083872`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29628143/).

Cellular stress recruited transport factors into stress granules and impaired nucleocytoplasmic transport. Altering stress-granule assembly modified transport defects and disease-model phenotypes. This provides a sequestration-based alternative to an intrinsic pore-modification hypothesis. Read alongside S3, it does not justify assuming that conventional stress granules are required for every TDP-43-associated transport defect.

## Evidence boundaries

- These selected passages do not establish that nucleoporin phosphorylation initiates ALS. Label a proposed kinase, modification site, or interaction as an assumption unless a supplied source supports it.
- Specify the ALS context; do not assume a universal mechanism across genetic and sporadic disease.
- Distinguish pore alteration, transport-factor sequestration, and failure secondary to broader stress.
- Explain temporal and perturbational evidence that would distinguish cause from consequence.
- Propose a research hypothesis rather than claiming a mechanism or treatment has been validated.


Proposed answer (the answer to evaluate):
Hypothesis title: Stress-activated phosphorylation of the FG-nucleoporin NUP98 initiates nuclear transport failure upstream of TDP-43 condensate sequestration in TDP-43-positive ALS motor neurons.

Mechanism and corrected causal chain. In stressed motor neurons carrying TDP-43 pathology, a proline-directed neuronal kinase phosphorylates NUP98 at S/T-P motif clusters in its disordered FG/GLFG repeat region. These motifs are pre-specified as a class: proline-directed CDK-consensus and p38-MAPK-consensus S/T-P sites, overlapping the mitotic-disassembly phosphosites reported for NUP98 (unverified prior knowledge recalled from outside the packet). In interphase neurons, this phosphorylation weakens NUP98 attachment to the pore scaffold and destabilizes the FG permeability barrier, causing Ran-dependent import failure while export machinery continues operating. Because TDP-43 is a shuttling protein, sustained import failure against ongoing export depletes nuclear TDP-43, matching the import-attributed nuclear depletion in [S3], and drives cytoplasmic accumulation. Directionality is now an explicit, testable claim: early export should be comparatively preserved, checked with an NES-cargo export reporter. Phosphorylation is the initiating lesion; sequestration into stress granules [S4] or cytoplasmic TDP-43 assemblies [S3] is an amplifier or downstream consequence.

Supported premises (packet only). [S1] links TDP-43 pathology to nucleoporin mislocalization and transport failure in ALS models and tissue. [S2] shows transport disruption produces ALS-relevant phenotypes, including RanGAP mislocalization, and is manipulable in the C9orf72 context. [S3] shows stress-granule-independent cytoplasmic TDP-43 assemblies impair import and deplete nuclear TDP-43. [S4] shows stress-granule assembly itself disrupts transport, the competing sequestration route. No packet source establishes any nucleoporin phosphorylation event in ALS.

Speculative bridges (assumptions). (1) CDK1 phosphorylates NUP98 at S/T-P sites during mitotic pore disassembly; this is unverified prior knowledge, with no supplied evidence that interphase neuronal stress reuses these sites. (2) The neuronal actor is CDK5 or p38 (both proline-directed; p38 is stress-activated, unverified prior knowledge); kinase identity is an assumption resolved empirically. (3) That interphase site phosphorylation alone impairs import and temporally precedes nuclear TDP-43 loss are assumptions.

Discriminating strategy: a gated two-phase design. Phase 1, temporal site mapping: in iPSC motor neurons (inducible TDP-43 nuclear depletion and C9orf72-expansion lines, with isogenic controls), run time-resolved phosphoproteomics on nuclear-envelope/NUP98-enriched fractions and generate phospho-specific antibodies against residues nominated from mapped S/T-P sites, prioritizing any matching reported mitotic phosphosites. Acceptance criterion: phosphorylation rises before RanGAP mislocalization, import decline, and nuclear TDP-43 loss. If no site precedes the defects, the hypothesis stops here; knock-in arms are gated on these results rather than run independently, so the scaffold-versus-barrier question is interrogated only at residues with confirmed disease-course phosphorylation. Kinase nomination precedes inhibitor use: a kinase is accepted only when its Phase-1 activation kinetics match NUP98 phosphorylation kinetics, and genetic perturbation (knockdown or kinase-dead rescue) alters NUP98 phosphorylation and transport. Promiscuous p38/CDK-class inhibitors are treated as supporting, never discriminating, evidence; the window-of-inhibition experiment runs only after genetic validation. Phase 2, necessity and orthogonal sufficiency: (a) knock-in phospho-null (S-to-A) NUP98 at Phase-1-confirmed residues should preserve import reporters, nuclear TDP-43, and survival despite stress-granule or TDP-43-assembly formation. (b) Sufficiency does not hinge on mimicry: because S-to-E/D charge mimicry poorly models phosphorylation of a phase-separating FG nucleoporin, an orthogonal test recruits the genetically nominated kinase to the nuclear envelope (optogenetic or rapamycin-induced targeting via an inner-nuclear-membrane anchor) in healthy neurons; import must fail before detectable TDP-43 aggregation or stress-granule recruitment, with site occupancy confirmed by targeted mass spectrometry. A negative phospho-mimetic result alone is treated as a possible mutation artifact, not automatic falsification. (c) Dual live readouts in the same cells, NLS-import, NES-export, and condensate/stress-granule markers, test the corrected chain: acute perturbation of the genetically validated kinase should rescue import without requiring condensate dissolution, whereas rescue only upon dissolution supports sequestration-first models.

Alternative explanations discriminated: (a) sequestration-first via cytoplasmic TDP-43 condensates [S3] or stress granules [S4]; (b) occlusion-first via direct aggregate binding and mislocalization of pore components [S1]; (c) epiphenomenon, where kinase activation merely marks stress damage.

Falsifying observation (convergent, three-pronged): (i) Phase-1 mapping finds no NUP98 phosphorylation preceding transport defects; (ii) phospho-null knock-in fails to preserve transport under TDP-43 stress; (iii) the orthogonal sufficiency test, despite confirmed site occupancy, does not impair transport. A single negative result, especially a phospho-mimetic failure alone, is insufficient for falsification; together these outcomes would indicate pore phosphorylation is secondary to sequestration or stress.

Limitations. The kinase, exact residues, temporal precedence, and sufficiency remain assumptions, and the packet is not a comprehensive review. The hypothesis is restricted to TDP-43-positive ALS and does not claim universality; C9orf72 disease involves additional transport-affecting routes [S2]. iPSC motor-neuron immaturity, FG-nucleoporin redundancy, and cell heterogeneity constrain interpretation; negative results must be checked across multiple sites and patient lines.

Ranked proposal:
Stress-activated phosphorylation of the FG-nucleoporin NUP98 initiates nuclear transport failure upstream of TDP-43 condensate sequestration in TDP-43-positive ALS motor neurons
